arguments.title: The lockout violated Property Code Section 93.002 because the new key was conditioned on a fee that is not delinquent rent
arguments.summary: Section 93.002(f) requires that a new key be provided during business hours if the tenant pays the delinquent rent. Landlord's agent conditioned the key on payment of $7,717.50 plus a $1,500 'lockout and administrative fee' that appears nowhere in the lease. Conditioning re-entry on a non-rent charge is outside what the statute permits, which would make the exclusion unlawful and trigger the remedies in Section 93.002(g): recovery of possession or termination, actual damages, the greater of one month's rent or $500, attorney's fees, and costs, less sums owed.

refs.quote: a new key would be released only after payment of $7,717.50 plus a $1,500.00 "lockout and administrative fee"
The new key is required to be provided only during the tenant's regular business hours and only if the tenant pays the delinquent rent

assumptions: The telephone statement about the fee can be proven (Tenant's contemporaneous email is the only record).
evidentiary_weaknesses: The posted notice itself appears to have included a name and telephone number, which satisfies the posting requirement in subsection (f).
Section 93.002(h) allows the lease to supersede the statute to the extent of conflict; Landlord will argue Section 15.2 governs.
anticipated_counterarguments: Landlord may say the fee was a separate demand and the key was available upon payment of rent alone.
Landlord may argue Tenant was delinquent in 'at least part of the rent', so the exclusion itself was permitted.
arguments.confidence_rationale: The fee demand is documented in Tenant's own email and confirmed in substance by Landlord's reply, but the exact condition for release of the key rests on an oral exchange.

arguments.title: The $1,500 lockout and administrative fee is barred by Property Code Section 93.012
arguments.summary: Section 93.012(a) prohibits a landlord from assessing any charge other than rent or physical damage unless the amount or computation method is stated in the lease, an exhibit, or an amendment. The lease sets a 5% late charge in Section 4.3 and attorneys' fees in Section 24.2 but contains no lockout, locksmith, or administrative fee. The charge is therefore unenforceable.

refs.quote: unless the amount of the charge or the method by which the charge is to be computed is stated in the lease, an exhibit or attachment that is part of the lease, or an amendment to the lease
The administrative fee covers the locksmith and our staff time

assumptions: No amendment or exhibit (other than the unreviewed Exhibit C guaranty) adds such a fee.
evidentiary_weaknesses: Exhibit B (Rules and Regulations) and Exhibit C were not fully reviewed; a fee schedule could exist there.
anticipated_counterarguments: Landlord may characterize the fee as damages or costs recoverable under Section 15.2(d) or common law rather than a 'charge'. Section 93.012(b) preserves statutory and common-law remedies.
arguments.confidence_rationale: The statutory text is direct and the lease contains no such fee; the main uncertainty is the exhibits not in the file.

arguments.title: No Event of Default existed when the locks were changed because written notice was not given in the manner the lease requires
arguments.summary: Section 15.1(a) requires written notice and a ten-day cure before a payment failure becomes an Event of Default, and Section 15.2 allows a lock change only 'upon an Event of Default'. Under Section 17.1 notice is given by personal delivery, overnight courier, or certified mail, and Section 17.2 says email is not notice unless receipt is acknowledged in a written reply. Tenant denies receiving the certified letter and Landlord has produced no receipt. If notice was given only by email, the cure period never started and the lock change on August 26 was premature under the lease itself.

refs.quote: shall not constitute notice under this Lease unless the receiving party expressly acknowledges receipt in a written reply
We never received any certified letter

assumptions: Landlord cannot produce a certified mail receipt or tracking showing mailing on or about August 11.
evidentiary_weaknesses: If Landlord mailed the notice on August 11, Section 17.1 deems it given three business days later regardless of actual receipt, and ten days from then would still have run before August 26.
Tenant's own August 26 email refers to 'the August 11 email attachment', which Landlord may call a written acknowledgment under Section 17.2.
anticipated_counterarguments: Deemed-delivery under Section 17.1(c) does not depend on receipt.
Section 93.002(c)(3) permits a lock change for delinquency independent of lease notice provisions, subject to subsection (h).
arguments.confidence_rationale: The argument turns entirely on whether certified mailing occurred, which is unknown, and faces a deemed-delivery clause.

arguments.title: Landlord bears responsibility for the rooftop HVAC unit as a Building System, entitling Tenant to reimbursement of the $8,400
arguments.summary: Section 1.10 defines Building Systems to include HVAC systems 'including rooftop equipment', and Section 7.1 makes Landlord responsible for Building Systems. Section 2.2 shows the parties treated the HVAC unit as something Landlord warranted at commencement. Reading the lease as a whole, the rooftop compressor is Landlord's to replace; Tenant gave written notice on June 10 and June 21, Landlord refused, and Tenant performed the repair. Tenant is entitled to reimbursement under Section 7.4 or damages under Section 91.004 and the lease.

refs.quote: including rooftop equipment, risers, and distribution lines up to the point of connection to the Premises
Landlord represents that the heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning unit serving the Premises shall be in good working order on the Commencement Date

assumptions: The replaced unit sits on the roof and connects to the Premises through building distribution lines.
The June 21 email counts as written notice despite Section 17.2, or Landlord's June 12 and June 20 replies amount to written acknowledgment.
evidentiary_weaknesses: Section 7.2 specifically assigns 'HVAC equipment exclusively serving the Premises' to Tenant, and the vendor described the unit as 'serving Suite 140'.
Section 1.10 limits Building Systems to systems serving the Building 'generally'.
No invoice or proof of payment is in the file.
Section 7.4 required an additional ten days' written notice of intent to repair; Tenant acted within days.
anticipated_counterarguments: Specific provisions (7.2) control over general definitions (1.10).
Even if Landlord owed the repair, Section 7.4 and Section 4.4 bar offset against rent, so Tenant's remedy was an invoice and a damages claim, not withholding.
arguments.confidence_rationale: The lease language genuinely cuts both ways; the specific-controls-general canon and the 'exclusively serving' wording weigh against Tenant, and the notice procedure was not followed precisely.

overall_assessment: Tenant's strongest, most conventional positions concern the manner of the lockout (the unauthorized fee and the key-release condition) rather than the underlying rent dispute. The HVAC responsibility argument is colorable but contested by specific lease text, and the offset was almost certainly prohibited by Sections 4.4 and 7.4 even if Landlord owed the repair.
